newsitem.title: JAPAN: Key overnight offer rate eases after BOJ operation.
newsitem.headline: Key overnight offer rate eases after BOJ operation.

text.p: Offering rates of the key overnight call rate eased on Monday after the Bank of Japan (BOJ) conducted a more accommodative operation than expected.
The operation was aimed at easing fund demand from banks on what is the last day of the fiscal year, traders said.
The BOJ left a surplus of 300 billion yen in the money market by draining 900 billion. Before the operation, the market had been in surplus by an estimated 1.2 trillion yen.
The key overnight rate was offered at around 0.65 percent while bids stood at 0.58 percent at 0040 GMT. The offer rate was around 0.70 percent just before the operation.
The weighted average of the key overnight rate was at 0.51 percent on Friday.
Traders said they had expected the BOJ to leave a surplus of 100 billion or 200 billion yen in Monday's operation.

"There had been expectations that the BOJ might leave a surplus of as much as 200 billion yen today as it is the fiscal year-end. But the surplus of 300 billion yen was even larger than that," said a commercial bank dealer.
A trust bank dealer said offers and bids will remain wide apart until the results of the BOJ's bill-selling operation are unveiled.
The BOJ said at 0020 GMT it had offered to sell two lots of bills totalling 900 billion yen via auctions.
Some 400 billion yen worth of bills mature on April 9 and the rest mature on April 11, the BOJ said.
"If operators fail to buy the total amount of bills, that would leave a greater surplus in the market. But if all bills are sold, the surplus will be 300 billion," the trust bank dealer said.
